title: AI is forcing us to pay off 40 years of technical debt
titleZh: AI is forcing us to pay off 40 years of technical debt
author: pseudolus
relevanceReason: 命中 4 个 AI/科技关键词。
summaryRaw: In late October, a slew of major cybersecurity issues came to light. But none were bigger than the so-called PHP2Shell vulnerability, which put a plethora of websites, including those of NASA, Wikipedia, the White House, and all other sites that run on Wordpress or Drupal (among others) at risk of exploits capable of both reading sensitive data and running malicious code on the host server.As far as anyone is aware, disaster has been averted: The hack was discovered by cybersecurity researchers who reported it to the PHP Foundation, and a patch was released before any bad actors got their hands on the exploit. However, PHP2Shell may be the canary in the coal mine, serving as a warning sign for what’s to come in the age of AI.“One of the things we’re witnessing now is that all the legacy software that was written by humans over the last 40 years is being exposed,” says Matt Suiche, AI security research lead at the cybersecurity startup Tolmo. “Now it is time for the technical debt to be paid off.”PHP Legacy Bug and Memory ErrorsPHP, which originally stood for “personal home page,” is a programming language created back in 1994 and largely used by legacy sites. The bug underlying the PHP2Shell vulnerability was reported to the PHP Foundation as far back as 2024. The bug caused a common type of issue called an out-of-memory error, in which the amount of memory allocated to a piece of data is too small to hold the data. Normally, this type of error causes the program to crash—an unpleasant but not inherently dangerous result. And so the bug remained unaddressed.“If you look at any at any point of time, there will be a bunch of bug reports that are waiting to be fixed, which are just crashes. Most people don’t take them very seriously,” says Suman Jana, an associate professor of computer science at Columbia University.“It’s just that it’s a lot of very specific reasoning that is painful to do. And AI, I think, has done a very good job at that.” –Suman Jana, Columbia UniversityEarlier this year, the cybersecurity firm Calif offered to independently audit PHP, sponsored by OpenAI. Within two weeks, a researcher at Calif, aided by AI tools, found a way to use the out-of-memory bug to run arbitrary code on the host server, allowing a malicious actor to install malware or read critical data. Now, it was no longer a minor bug—it was a critical vulnerability, and the Calif team alerted the PHP foundation to start working on a patch immediately.Jana says actually exploiting the bug requires carefully working out a way to jump to a specific point in the memory for a particular program running on the server, and work out exactly which bits to overwrite in what order to gain control of the system. “It’s not really rocket science,” he says. “It’s just that it’s a lot of very specific reasoning that is painful to do. And AI, I think, has done a very good job at that.”To be clear, the researchers at Calif (as well as OpenAI and Wiz, a cybersecurity company that confirmed and expanded the vulnerabilities) had deep knowledge of both cybersecurity and the PHP language. “I’m not claiming that AI can do it all by itself. It clearly cannot,” Jana says. “But it is improving a lot, so the top 0.1 percent [of experts] can get a lot more stuff done, and also just below the 0.1 percent now will be able to go there without understanding all the nitty-gritty details.”AI Tools and Formal Verification in SecurityAfter the exploits were disclosed to the PHP Foundation, a team of four engineers spent two months developing a patch to release as quickly as possible.“There is a fundamental asymmetry in finding bugs and fixing bugs,” Jana says. “Because when you’re fixing bugs you have to make sure that you know all parts of that attack are closed, and also that you don’t break any existing functionality.”This asymmetry puts a lot of strain on the defenders, especially for open-source software such as PHP. Maintaining open-source projects that don’t have clear revenue streams despite being widely used is a long-standing challenge that precedes AI hacking tools. But those tools make the issue more pressing than ever. One way to stay ahead of such issues going forward is to empower the defenders with more money and access to frontier cybersecurity AI models. “These frontier labs are donating some of their token budgets to look into these bugs, which I think is great,” Jana says. “I think that should happen more, either through some concerted effort or through donations.”Jana is also optimistic that formal verification tools to automate the patching side of the equation are also advancing quickly, including a new release from Anthropic on 22 October. “The patch is LLM-generated, and then an LLM generates the proof that the patch is correct,” says Jana. “The only thing not done by an LLM is the proof checker, because somebody has to check the proof, because LLMs hallucinate. So, you want something that is formal.”Hopefully, the combination of specialized AI models and formal verification tools will make patching vulnerabilities nearly as automatable as finding them. Matthew Green, an associate professor of computer science at Johns Hopkins University Information Security Institute, is less optimistic. “Nobody’s going to fix this problem until something really bad happens,” he says. “And PHP2Shell wasn’t bad enough to be really bad. So when something really bad happens, which is going to be maybe sometime in early 2027, something bad that normal people are upset by, then suddenly people will start doing this. We’re going to fund everything.”In the meantime, Green says, update your software. “If your phone is like, ‘Hey, there’s a security update available, do you want to install it,’ don’t wait till next week. Just do it.”One thing’s for sure—PHP2Shell is just the beginning. “This won’t be the last one for sure,” Jana says. “It’s just who finds it. Hopefully, the white-hat hackers find it first, like this one.”

comments.author: Arbortheus
comments.textRawHtml:
I hope some of these backdoors and/or 0-days being kept under wraps by nation states or corporate espionage companies (Pegasus et al) are being found incidentally through all this.

It’s frustrating to have all these 0days and CVEs to patch for now, but in the long run perhaps we’ll leave with more robust software.

children.author: Loquebantur
children.textRawHtml:
The logical extrapolation of AI capabilities stress-testing human software is all bugs being discoverable. Hence, you have to aim for actually bug-free software.

The only way to do that is to make your code provable. That again is only realistically doable using AI.

In the process, people will have to turn the pretense of "software engineering" into reality, making the engineering part explicit.

That only works when humans actually understand what they're doing.

children.author: Quimoniz
children.textRawHtml:
> "I have only proven [my code] correct, not bug free."

> -- Donald Knuth (if I recall that exact quote correctly)

Just because you have proven the correctness of your code, that does not mean that it is infallible. Especially -- as a lot of HN users point out -- there's intricate complexity that is likely to cause erroneous behavior if several interfaces/complexities get combined. And those might be caused, for example by a 'user' setting the driver to 'db.backend.sqlite' instead of 'db.backend.sqlite3'; and then you have suddenly an unexpected configuration.

children.author: phorkyas82
children.textRawHtml:
Were you aiming for this? “Program testing can be used to show the presence of bugs, but never to show their absence!” ― Edsger W. Dijkstra

Or the second one, that I would have attributed to Dijkstra, too: “There are two ways of constructing a software design: One way is to make it so simple that there are obviously no deficiencies and the other way is to make it so complicated that there are no obvious deficiencies.” C.A.R. Hoare, The 1980 ACM Turing Award Lecture

children.author: svachalek
children.textRawHtml: This doesn't necessarily require proving everything mathematically, it also helps to design things in a way that doesn't rely on discipline to avoid gaping holes. For example, languages that allow pointer arithmetic, unchecked array access, or use-after-free have huge opportunities to make security errors that don't exist in languages without them.

children.author: hinkley
children.textRawHtml:
A problem I frequently have with setting up testing policies is in convincing people to test what they can reliably test with the tools, and know what they cannot test.

Inconclusive tests to increase automation and coverage accomplish less than nothing. The opportunity cost, the loss of trust, the conflation of the manual testing surface area, are all worse than doing nothing.

The point of testing is to establish a level of trust. That level doesn’t need to be 100%. It can’t be 100% regardless. So you do what you can, and you solve the remaining problem a different way. But you need to know it’s there to address it, and the smoke and mirrors fight that.

children.author: annzabelle
children.textRawHtml:
I used to work for a company that enforced 80% code coverage for our CI/CD pipelines. Both teams I worked with there, in wildly different parts of the company, were playing games with excluding most files in the repo and writing dozens of tests that didn't actually test anything, just ran the code in the testing container so the lines would count as having been tested. I think LLMs have probably cleaned it all up a lot in the end, because the tests they write do actually test the code (against the code at the point you told the LLM to write the test a lot of the time, rather than a third party spec, but at least it's not just return true all the time).

Every 6 months there was a new testing initiative, which seemed to all be responded to by writing wrappers that returned true to the test automation system we were ordered to use.
